headline: Connecticut awards $6.2M to 29 districts to improve student attendance
dek: The new grants expand a home-visiting program that state officials say helped drive four straight years of lower chronic absenteeism, but the latest awards will still have to translate into local services.
body: Connecticut is awarding approximately $6.2 million to 29 school districts and regional education organizations for a home-visiting program aimed at bringing chronically absent students back into regular contact with their schools.

The grants, announced Sept. 30 by Gov. Ned Lamont and Education Commissioner Charlene Russell-Tucker, are being distributed through the Learner Engagement and Attendance Program, known as LEAP. The money comes from a $7 million state budget line item. About $800,000 will support statewide infrastructure such as home-visitor training, program implementation and data collection, according to the [Connecticut governor’s announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/09-2026/governor-lamont-and-commissioner-russell-tucker-announce-state-grants-to-expand-program).

LEAP pairs trained school staff and community partners with students and families. The visits are intended to identify the practical or personal barriers behind missed school days and connect families with services that can make regular attendance possible. The program began in 2021 with federal pandemic-relief money, initially serving 15 districts. It later expanded to 25, and this round brings the state’s reach to 29 districts for the 2026-27 school year.

The recipients include some of Connecticut’s largest districts. Waterbury is slated to receive $525,000, Hartford $500,000, Bridgeport $475,000 and New Haven $425,000. Stamford will receive $350,000, while smaller awards go to districts including East Windsor, East Haven, Plainfield and Jamestown. Middletown’s $125,000 award was reported separately by [Middletown Patch](https://patch.com/connecticut/middletown-ct/middletown-school-system-getting-6-figure-grant-aimed-boosting-attendance), which described the grant as funding for the same statewide LEAP effort.

State officials say Connecticut’s chronic-absenteeism rate fell from 23.7% in the 2021-22 school year to 16.4% in 2025-26. The governor’s office calculated that change as nearly 35,000 more students attending school regularly than at the earlier point. The figures describe statewide movement and do not establish that LEAP alone caused the decline; the announcement calls the program one part of a broader attendance strategy.

There is earlier research behind the state’s decision to continue the program. The Center for Connecticut Education Research Collaboration, a partnership involving the state education department and Connecticut colleges, studied LEAP’s first 15 districts. Its [published evaluation](https://portal.ct.gov/ccerc/current-projects/leap) found attendance gains after home visits, including an average increase of nearly 15 percentage points six months after visits for students served during the 2021-22 school year. The study also reported different effects by grade level and district, which matters because the new grant round includes a broader mix of communities than the initial cohort.

Connecticut says home visitors have conducted about 88,000 visits and reached roughly 53,000 students since LEAP began. Those totals are cumulative program figures supplied by the state, not an independent count released with the new awards. The current announcement also does not provide a district-by-district attendance target or a deadline for demonstrating results.

The immediate test will be local execution. Districts will need to recruit or assign visitors, train them, coordinate with community organizations and turn conversations with families into help with transportation, health, housing, counseling or other barriers when those needs are identified. If the grants produce lasting attendance gains, Connecticut will have a stronger case for making the home-visiting model a durable part of school operations after the pandemic-era funding that launched it has faded.
author: NorthEast News Desk
